Break or chop the chancaca into pieces. Combine with water, cinnamon stick, cloves, and orange peel in a saucepan. Heat over medium, stirring to dissolve the sugar. Once dissolved, bring to a gentle boil and cook for 10-12 minutes until syrupy and fragrant. Strain out the spices and peel. Keep warm. The syrup should be dark, spiced, and thick enough to drizzle.

Heat the oil to 175°C (345°F) in a deep, wide pan. Wet your hands thoroughly. Grab a golf ball-sized portion of dough, poke a hole through the center with your finger, and stretch into a ring shape (about 10cm diameter) directly over the hot oil. Drop it in. Fry in batches of 3-4, turning once after 2-3 minutes, until both sides are deep golden-brown. Total frying time is 4-5 minutes per batch. The dough will expand in the oil. Drain on paper towels.

recipes.title: Pico de Gallo
recipes.summary: Mexico's fresh, chunky tomato salsa — ripe tomato, white onion, jalapeño, cilantro, and lime juice cut fine and macerated just long enough for the juices to pool in the bowl.
recipes.description: Mexico's fresh, chunky tomato salsa — ripe tomato, white onion, jalapeño, cilantro, and lime juice cut fine and macerated just long enough for the juices to pool in the bowl.

ingredients.name: Ripe Roma or vine tomatoes, seeds removed, fine dice
Jalapeño or serrano, seeds and ribs removed for medium heat, minced
Fresh cilantro, leaves and tender stems, chopped

steps.instruction: This is a knife-skill recipe. Begin with the onion: dice it very fine (3–4 mm), then place in a small bowl and rinse with cold water to reduce the harsh raw bite — squeeze dry in a paper towel. Core and halve the tomatoes, scoop out the seeds and gel with a spoon (this prevents the finished salsa from becoming watery), then dice the flesh into 5–8 mm pieces — not too fine or the salsa turns mushy, not too coarse or it won't coat a chip. Mince the jalapeño as fine as possible; start with only half if uncertain about heat level. Chop the cilantro coarsely — it will macerate and soften, so you don't want it minced to nothing.

Combine all the diced vegetables in a bowl. Add the cilantro, lime juice, and salt. Fold gently with a spoon — do not stir vigorously or the tomatoes will break down. Taste immediately: the lime should be assertive and the salt should pop everything forward. Do not under-salt; pico de gallo needs more salt than feels comfortable when tasting from a plain spoon because it is served with unsalted tortilla chips or plain corn. Let the pico sit for 10 minutes before serving so the salt draws out the tomato juices and they pool in the bowl, creating a natural light brine.

recipes.title: Piri Piri Sauce
recipes.summary: A vivid, oil-bright red sauce from the African bird's eye chili — simultaneously fiery and fruity, with a lemon-garlic sharpness that makes grilled chicken sing and your lips tingle long after the last bite.
recipes.description: A vivid, oil-bright red sauce from the African bird's eye chili — simultaneously fiery and fruity, with a lemon-garlic sharpness that makes grilled chicken sing and your lips tingle long after the last bite.

ingredients.name: Bird's eye chilies (fresh or dried and rehydrated), stems removed
Red bell pepper, roughly chopped and roasted

steps.instruction: Place the red bell pepper pieces and whole garlic cloves on a baking tray under a very hot broiler (240C/460F) or directly over a gas flame using tongs. Roast until the pepper skin is blackened and blistered in patches and the garlic is golden-brown and soft inside. The pepper takes 10-15 minutes, the garlic 8-10 minutes. Transfer to a bowl, cover with cling film, and steam for 5 minutes. Peel the pepper skin off — the char and steam loosens it.

Combine the chilies, peeled roasted pepper, roasted garlic, lemon juice, vinegar, oil, salt, oregano, and paprika in a blender or food processor. Blend on high for 2 minutes until completely smooth and emulsified. If the sauce is too thick, add a tablespoon of water and blend again. Taste carefully — the heat will be significant. Adjust with more lemon for brightness or more salt for depth.

For a cooked piri piri (preferred for marinating and shelf stability): pour the blended sauce into a small saucepan and simmer over low heat for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Cooking mellows the raw chili edge, deepens the roasted pepper flavor, and extends refrigerator life to 2 weeks. For a fresh, vibrant table sauce, skip this step and use raw. Cool completely before jarring.

recipes.title: Pistou
recipes.summary: Provence's uncooked basil paste — raw garlic pounded with fresh basil and olive oil into a vivid green sauce that smells like a garden in August. Unlike its Ligurian cousin pesto, pistou contains no nuts and no cheese, meaning all the flavors are immediate and transparent, with nowhere for the basil to hide.
recipes.description: Provence's uncooked basil paste — raw garlic pounded with fresh basil and olive oil into a vivid green sauce that smells like a garden in August. Unlike its Ligurian cousin pesto, pistou contains no nuts and no cheese, meaning all the flavors are immediate and transparent, with nowhere for the basil to hide.

steps.instruction: In a mortar, pound the garlic cloves with the coarse salt until a completely smooth, white paste forms. The salt crystals act as an abrasive and draw out the moisture from the garlic. This step is crucial — any remaining garlic chunks will make the sauce harsh and unpleasant. If using a food processor instead, mince the garlic as fine as possible before proceeding.

Add basil leaves to the mortar in two or three batches. Pound and grind with a circular pressing motion — not sharp strikes — until each batch is completely incorporated before adding the next. The goal is to bruise and crush the cells to release the oils, not to create friction heat. If using a food processor, pulse briefly in short bursts — blending too long heats the basil and turns it black.

Stream in olive oil a little at a time, stirring and pressing the paste against the sides of the mortar to incorporate. The sauce will loosen and become glossy as the oil emulsifies with the water content of the basil. Add a small squeeze of lemon juice if using. The consistency should be thick enough to coat a spoon but fluid enough to pour. Use immediately — pistou begins to oxidize and lose its vivid color within 30 minutes.

recipes.title: Preserved Lemons
recipes.summary: Whole lemons packed tight in their own juice with coarse salt and spices, sealed in a jar and left for a month — transforming the rind from bitter pith to a silky, mellow, intensely savory and fragrant preserve.
recipes.description: Whole lemons packed tight in their own juice with coarse salt and spices, sealed in a jar and left for a month — transforming the rind from bitter pith to a silky, mellow, intensely savory and fragrant preserve.

ingredients.name: Coarse non-iodized sea salt or kosher salt
Fresh lemon juice (from additional lemons for brine)

steps.instruction: Scrub the lemons thoroughly under warm water to remove any surface wax or pesticide residue — unwaxed lemons are strongly preferred, as the rind is the prize and you want nothing between the salt and the natural lemon oils. Cut each lemon nearly into quarters from the top, stopping 1–2 cm before the base so the lemon holds together in a fan shape. This quartered-but-hinged cut maximizes the surface area exposed to the salt while keeping the lemon whole for an attractive presentation. Pack 1–2 tablespoons of coarse salt generously into the opening of each quartered lemon, pressing the salt into the flesh. The quantity of salt is not negotiable — undersalting will allow harmful bacterial growth rather than the desired fermentation.

Sterilize a wide-mouth glass jar (large enough to hold all the lemons tightly) by boiling or running through a dishwasher's hot cycle. Place a bay leaf, a small piece of cinnamon, a pinch of peppercorns, and the cloves in the base of the jar. Pack the salt-stuffed lemons into the jar as tightly as possible, squeezing them in and pressing down so the lemons compress and release their juice. Tuck additional spices between the lemons as you layer. Once all lemons are packed, press down firmly with your fist — you want the jar to be so tight the lemons cannot rattle or move. Pour fresh lemon juice over the top until the lemons are fully submerged. If needed, add a small amount of additional salt dissolved in lemon juice. Seal tightly.

Store the sealed jar at room temperature (18–24°C / 65–75°F) for 30 days minimum, turning the jar upside down once daily for the first week to redistribute the salt and juices, ensuring all lemon surfaces are bathed in the brine. The lemons will gradually sink as they soften and the juice level will look different from day to day — this is normal. After a week, the turning is less critical, but occasional rotation helps. At 30 days, taste: the rind should be tender, translucent, and mellow — not sharply bitter but savory-salty-fragrant. The flesh is typically discarded when using preserved lemons in cooking; only the rind is used.

Once cured, refrigerate the jar. To use: remove a lemon quarter, rinse the salt from the rind under cold water, then scrape away and discard the flesh and pith — only the silky, translucent rind is used. Slice or mince the rind and use in tagines, grain salads, pasta, compound butters, or dressings. The brine in the jar is also excellent: use it as a seasoning salt substitute in sauces and braises. Preserved lemons can transform a dish from good to memorable with just a small amount — their flavor is concentrated, so use with restraint until you understand their potency.

recipes.title: Provençal Tian
recipes.summary: Rounds of zucchini, ripe tomato, and waxy potato arranged in overlapping spirals in an olive-oil-slicked earthenware dish, then baked until every edge catches colour and the vegetables melt into each other at their touching faces.
recipes.description: Rounds of zucchini, ripe tomato, and waxy potato arranged in overlapping spirals in an olive-oil-slicked earthenware dish, then baked until every edge catches colour and the vegetables melt into each other at their touching faces.

ingredients.name: Ripe plum tomatoes, sliced 5 mm rounds
Waxy potato, peeled, sliced 5 mm rounds
Fresh thyme and rosemary, stripped from stems
Flaky sea salt and black pepper

steps.instruction: Use a mandoline or very sharp knife to slice all vegetables to a uniform 5 mm thickness. Consistency is what makes the tian visually cohesive — irregular slices bake unevenly, leaving raw patches beside overdone edges. Lay slices on a clean surface and assess for uniformity.

Coat the bottom of a wide earthenware gratin dish with a third of the olive oil. Scatter garlic slices across the oil. Arrange the vegetable rounds standing upright in overlapping rows — potato, zucchini, tomato, repeating — tilting each round slightly so it leans on the one behind it. Drizzle the remaining olive oil over the top, scatter herbs throughout the slices, and season generously with flaky salt and pepper.

Cover the dish with foil and bake at 180 C (350 F) for 40 minutes to steam the vegetables through. Remove the foil and raise the oven to 220 C (425 F). Bake a further 25–35 minutes until the tops are deeply golden and the tomato has caramelised at its edges. The dish should be bubbling gently at the perimeter. Rest 10 minutes before serving.

recipes.title: Quick Shio-Koji Tsukemono
recipes.summary: Crisp, lightly salted Japanese quick pickles cured with shio-koji — the enzymes in the rice koji tenderize and season vegetables in hours, not days, with a gentle umami depth.
recipes.description: Crisp, lightly salted Japanese quick pickles cured with shio-koji — the enzymes in the rice koji tenderize and season vegetables in hours, not days, with a gentle umami depth.

ingredients.name: Japanese cucumber (or Persian cucumber), sliced on bias

steps.instruction: Slice the cucumber on the bias into 5mm-thick ovals — the angled cut increases the surface area exposed to the cure and looks elegant. Cut the daikon into 5mm half-moons. Combine all the prepared vegetables in a mixing bowl, sprinkle with the fine sea salt, and toss gently to distribute. Let them sit for 10 minutes. The initial salt draw is rapid: you will see brine beginning to pool in the bowl within 5 minutes. This step pre-softens the cell walls and removes some bitterness from the daikon, giving the shio-koji a better surface to work with. After 10 minutes, rinse the vegetables briefly under cold water and pat them dry with a clean cloth — you want to remove the harsh drawn liquid before adding the subtler shio-koji.

In the bowl with the dried vegetables, add the shio-koji, julienned ginger, and rice vinegar. Toss with clean hands, massaging the shio-koji into the vegetables so every surface is coated with the white, paste-like koji. The shio-koji looks like a thick, grain-studded paste — the rice particles are the koji, teeming with protease and amylase enzymes that will break down the vegetable surface proteins and starches, creating depth and umami that straight salt cannot produce. Massage for about 1 minute until the shio-koji is evenly distributed and no white clumps remain. Transfer to a sealable bag or a container with a weight on top.

Seal the bag or cover the container and press the vegetables flat (use a plate and a heavy jar as a weight if using a bowl). Refrigerate for a minimum of 1 hour, but 2 hours is optimal for this quick style. After 1 hour, taste a piece — the seasoning should be evenly distributed from surface to center, and the vegetables should taste mildly fermented, savory, and gently sweet from the koji's amylase activity. At 2 hours the flavor deepens noticeably; beyond 4 hours the texture begins to soften past ideal crunch, and by 24 hours you have a fuller, more deeply cured tsukemono with less crunch — still delicious but a different product.

Drain the cured vegetables and give them a brief, gentle rinse under cold water to remove excess koji paste and surface salt — this is a matter of taste and presentation. The Japanese convention for tsukemono is to arrange them in a small bowl or on a dish alongside rice, soup, and other dishes, using them as a palate-cleansing accent rather than a main element. Serve at room temperature or lightly chilled. Store remaining tsukemono in the fridge in the brine for up to 3 days — the flavor will continue to develop and deepen each day. By day 3 they will be more assertively fermented and less crisp, which is a different pleasure.

recipes.title: Quinoa Tabbouleh
recipes.summary: A gluten-free riff on the Levantine herb salad — cooked quinoa standing in for bulgur, but the spirit kept luminously intact: mostly flat-leaf parsley and fresh mint, punctuated by sweet tomato and cool cucumber, all dressed generously in sharp lemon and grassy olive oil.
recipes.description: A gluten-free riff on the Levantine herb salad — cooked quinoa standing in for bulgur, but the spirit kept luminously intact: mostly flat-leaf parsley and fresh mint, punctuated by sweet tomato and cool cucumber, all dressed generously in sharp lemon and grassy olive oil.

ingredients.name: Ripe tomatoes, seeded and finely diced
Persian or English cucumber, finely diced

steps.instruction: Rinse the quinoa under cold running water for a full 60 seconds in a fine-mesh sieve, rubbing the grains between your palms. This removes the bitter saponin coating. Combine with the water in a small saucepan and bring to a boil over medium heat. Reduce to the lowest simmer, cover, and cook 12–14 minutes until all water is absorbed. Remove from heat and let steam, covered, for 5 minutes. Then tip onto a large tray or baking sheet and spread into a thin layer to cool completely to room temperature — adding warm quinoa to the salad will wilt the herbs and cook the vegetables.

The knife work here makes or breaks tabbouleh. Strip the parsley leaves from their stems (save stems for stock) and chop very finely — almost to a near-paste in texture, not a rough chop. The mint should be treated the same way. Dice the seeded tomatoes and cucumber to a uniformly fine dice, roughly 5mm. Slice the scallions thinly, including most of the green tops. Tabbouleh is a parsley salad with other ingredients; if the quinoa is dominant, you've made a grain bowl. Parsley should be the visual and volumetric majority.

In a large bowl, combine the cooled quinoa with the chopped herbs, tomatoes, cucumber and scallions. Drizzle over the lemon juice and olive oil, season with salt and pepper, and toss gently but thoroughly. Taste and adjust — authentic tabbouleh is assertively lemony and well-salted; it should make your eyes water slightly with the brightness of lemon. Let rest at room temperature for 10–15 minutes before serving — this brief rest allows the quinoa to absorb the dressing and the flavors to marry.

recipes.title: Ras el Hanout
recipes.summary: Morocco's "top of the shop" spice blend — a sweeping mix of up to 30 warm spices toasted and ground together, from rose petals to black cardamom to mace, layered in ways that deepen every tagine and couscous it touches.
recipes.description: Morocco's "top of the shop" spice blend — a sweeping mix of up to 30 warm spices toasted and ground together, from rose petals to black cardamom to mace, layered in ways that deepen every tagine and couscous it touches.

steps.instruction: Place a wide, dry skillet over medium heat and let it warm for two minutes. Add all the whole spices — cumin seeds, coriander seeds, black peppercorns, green and black cardamom seeds (cracked out of their pods), cinnamon stick broken into pieces, dried ginger, cloves, mace blades, and allspice berries — in a single layer. Toast, shaking the pan every 20–30 seconds, for 3–5 minutes total. You are not looking for color change so much as fragrance activation: the moment the kitchen fills with a warm, complex, resinous aroma that smells like a Moroccan souk, you are there. The spices should feel warm and dry to the touch when you pinch one between your fingers. Remove from the heat immediately and tip onto a cool plate — do not leave them in the hot pan, as carryover heat will tip them into bitterness.

Let the toasted spices cool for five minutes — grinding hot spices in a electric grinder creates steam that clumps the powder. Add the toasted spices to a spice grinder or powerful blender along with the ground turmeric, hot paprika, ground nutmeg, and dried rose petals. Grind in 15-second bursts, pausing to shake and redistribute between bursts, until you reach a fine, uniform powder with no visible whole spice pieces. If using a mortar, pound in stages: hardest spices first (peppercorns, cardamom, cloves), then softer (cinnamon, ginger, mace, allspice), then fold in the already-ground ingredients last. The rose petals are delicate — add them in the final pulse so they don't turn into sticky paste.

Tip the ground blend into a bowl. Smell it carefully, layer by layer — first the top notes (floral rose, peppery heat), then the middle (warm cumin and coriander), then the base (resinous cardamom and clove). Taste a pinch on the back of your hand. The blend should feel like a conversation where many voices are present but none is shouting: no single spice should dominate. If the pepper is overwhelming, add a little more coriander and cinnamon to soften it. If it's flat and one-dimensional, a touch more black cardamom or clove will deepen it. If it smells purely of cumin, add more coriander, paprika, and rose. Once balanced, stir to integrate any adjustments.

Transfer the finished ras el hanout into a clean, airtight glass jar or spice tin. Do not use a plastic container — plastic absorbs the volatile oils and the blend will fade quickly. Press out any air before sealing. Label with the date. Store in a cool, dark place — a drawer or spice cabinet away from the stove is ideal. Heat and light are the enemies of complex spice blends. At peak freshness, ras el hanout is revelatory; after three months it loses the floral and flint top-notes first, becoming progressively flatter. Use within three months for best results. As a rough guide: 1–2 teaspoons per 500g of meat in a tagine; 1 teaspoon per cup of couscous cooking water; a generous pinch per serving of roasted vegetables.

recipes.title: Ribollita
recipes.summary: A thick Tuscan peasant soup built from the bones of yesterday's bread and the season's darkest cavolo nero — re-boiled until the beans dissolve into the broth and the torn bread swells to a trembling, almost porridge-like consistency that a spoon stands up in.
recipes.description: A thick Tuscan peasant soup built from the bones of yesterday's bread and the season's darkest cavolo nero — re-boiled until the beans dissolve into the broth and the torn bread swells to a trembling, almost porridge-like consistency that a spoon stands up in.

ingredients.name: Stale Tuscan pane sciocco (unsalted bread), torn
Cavolo nero (lacinato kale), stems removed, roughly chopped
Canned whole San Marzano tomatoes, hand-crushed
Extra-virgin olive oil, plus more to finish
Fresh rosemary, sage, and thyme (tied into a bundle)
Fine sea salt and black pepper

steps.instruction: Drain the soaked beans and cover with fresh cold water by 5 cm in a large pot. Add the herb bundle and a generous pinch of salt. Bring to a boil, skim any grey foam that rises, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Cook for 60-90 minutes until the beans are completely tender throughout with no chalky center when bitten. Do not add acid (no tomato, no vinegar) until the beans are fully cooked — acid toughens bean skins. Reserve all the cooking liquid — it becomes the base of the soup. Remove the herb bundle. Roughly mash or blend one-third of the cooked beans directly in the pot to create body in the soup; leave two-thirds whole.

In a separate large, heavy pot, heat the olive oil over medium-low heat. Add the onion, celery, carrot, and garlic with a pinch of salt. Cook slowly for 12-15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the vegetables are completely soft, sweet-smelling, and lightly golden. This is the soffritto — the flavor foundation. The vegetables should be so soft they break apart when pressed with a spoon. Add the crushed tomatoes, stir in, and cook for another 5 minutes until the tomato has darkened slightly and smells sweet.

Add the cavolo nero leaves to the soffritto and stir until wilted, about 3 minutes. Pour in the cooked beans along with all their cooking liquid. Add more water or stock if needed — the mixture should be soupy, not stew-thick. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 25-30 minutes until the cavolo nero is completely tender and has lost its tough, fibrous quality. The broth should taste deeply savory and slightly sweet from the beans. Season generously with salt and pepper.

Tear the stale bread into large, rough chunks — about 5 cm pieces — and press them into the simmering soup. Do not stir immediately. Let the bread absorb the broth for 2-3 minutes, then stir gently to incorporate. The bread will swell dramatically and begin to fall apart, thickening the soup to a porridge-like consistency. Add more broth if the mixture becomes too thick to stir. Simmer for another 15-20 minutes on low heat, stirring regularly to prevent the bread from sticking to the bottom.

This is the step that gives ribollita its name — 're-boiled.' Bring the thick soup back to a lively simmer over medium heat, stirring frequently to prevent the bread-thickened base from scorching on the bottom. Simmer for 10 minutes. Taste and adjust salt generously — ribollita needs bold seasoning. Ladle into deep bowls. Finish each bowl with a generous pour of the best olive oil you have — it will pool on the surface and slowly sink in. Serve with a coarse grind of black pepper and, optionally, a slice of grilled bread across the top.

recipes.title: Salt-Crust Roasted Beets
recipes.summary: Whole beets buried in coarse salt and roasted low and slow until the salt draws moisture and the beet's natural sugars concentrate into an intense, jewel-bright sweetness — a technique that takes far longer than foil-roasting but produces a flavor that is categorically different.
recipes.description: Whole beets buried in coarse salt and roasted low and slow until the salt draws moisture and the beet's natural sugars concentrate into an intense, jewel-bright sweetness — a technique that takes far longer than foil-roasting but produces a flavor that is categorically different.

ingredients.name: Coarse sea salt or rock salt
Red wine vinegar or balsamic, for serving

steps.instruction: Pour half the coarse salt into a deep baking dish to create a 2 cm bed. Nestle the whole, unpeeled beets on the salt, spacing them so they do not touch. Pour the remaining salt over and around the beets to cover them completely — they should be fully buried with no beet surface visible. The salt draws moisture out slowly and creates a sealed, even-temperature cooking environment, concentrating sugars far more than conventional roasting.

Roast in a preheated 190 C (375 F) oven for 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours. The salt will partially harden into a crust. To test for doneness, push a thin metal skewer through the salt into the largest beet — it should pass through with no resistance, like pushing into room-temperature butter. Small beets take 80 minutes; very large ones may need 2 hours 15 minutes.

Crack the salt crust with a spoon and remove the beets. The skin will peel off in large pieces using just your fingers and a paper towel (wear gloves if you don't want to stain your hands deep red for a day). Slice, quarter, or serve whole. Dress immediately with olive oil and a few drops of red wine vinegar or balsamic to add brightness to the concentrated sweetness.

recipes.title: Roasted Cauliflower with Tahini Lentils
recipes.summary: Cumin-and-paprika cauliflower roasted until the edges char sweet and nutty, piled over earthy lentils dressed in a lemony, garlicky tahini. Warm, creamy, and bright with a heap of fresh parsley.
recipes.description: Cumin-and-paprika cauliflower roasted until the edges char sweet and nutty, piled over earthy lentils dressed in a lemony, garlicky tahini. Warm, creamy, and bright with a heap of fresh parsley.

ingredients.name: Cauliflower, cut into 4 cm florets (1 large head)
Garlic, 1 smashed whole and 1 finely grated
Lemon juice (about 1.5 lemons), plus zest of 1

steps.instruction: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Toss the florets with 45 ml of the oil, the cumin, paprika, and 1 teaspoon salt. Spread on a large sheet pan with cut sides down and space between pieces. Roast 25–30 minutes, flipping once at 15 minutes, until tender and well charred at the edges.

While the cauliflower roasts, put the lentils, bay leaf, and the smashed garlic clove in a saucepan with the water. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer and cook 20–25 minutes until tender but holding their shape. Salt the water in the last 5 minutes. Drain, discard the bay and garlic.

Whisk the tahini with the lemon juice, the grated garlic clove, and a pinch of salt. It will seize and thicken — keep going. Add the ice water a tablespoon at a time, whisking until it lightens to a smooth, pourable sauce.

Toss the warm lentils with half the tahini sauce, the remaining 15 ml olive oil, the lemon zest, and half the parsley. Season with salt. Spread on a platter, top with the roasted cauliflower, drizzle over the remaining tahini, and finish with almonds and the rest of the parsley.

recipes.title: Roasted Vegetable Stock
recipes.summary: Onion, carrot, celery, leek, fennel, and mushroom skins roasted to deep golden-brown and then simmered with herbs and black peppercorns — the roasting gives this vegan stock a depth and body that makes it genuinely useful in place of light meat stocks.
recipes.description: Onion, carrot, celery, leek, fennel, and mushroom skins roasted to deep golden-brown and then simmered with herbs and black peppercorns — the roasting gives this vegan stock a depth and body that makes it genuinely useful in place of light meat stocks.

ingredients.name: Dried mushroom skins or shiitake stems (or 30g dried porcini)
Bay leaves, flat-leaf parsley stems, fresh thyme

steps.instruction: Preheat oven to 220°C (425°F). Spread all vegetables on two large sheet pans — do not crowd them. Drizzle with oil and toss to coat. Dot the tomato paste in spoonfuls across the vegetables. Roast for 35–40 minutes, tossing once at the 20-minute mark, until the vegetables are deeply caramelized and dark at the edges — golden-brown onions, nearly blackened carrot edges, dark-spotted leeks. The deeper the color here, the richer and more complex the stock.

Remove the pans from the oven. Add a small amount of cold water (about 2 tablespoons per pan) to each hot pan and scrape vigorously with a wooden spoon or spatula to dissolve all the dark caramelized fond from the pan surface. This concentrated caramelized material is extremely rich in Maillard reaction products and is a primary driver of stock depth.

Transfer all roasted vegetables and deglaze liquid to a large stockpot. Add dried mushrooms, herb bundle, peppercorns, and cold water. Bring to a boil, then immediately reduce to a bare simmer — just occasional bubbles breaking the surface. Simmer for 1 hour 30 minutes. Skim any foam that forms in the first 15 minutes. Do not stir — stirring makes the stock cloudy. Do not let it boil hard at any point after the initial come-up.

Set a fine-mesh sieve over a large bowl or pot. Ladle the stock through the sieve — do not pour directly from the pot, which would force cloudy liquid through. Do not press the vegetables. Let gravity drain the stock for 5 minutes. Discard the exhausted vegetables. Allow stock to cool at room temperature for 1 hour, then refrigerate. Skim any oil from the surface when cold. Use within 5 days or freeze in 500ml portions for up to 6 months.

recipes.title: Romesco Sauce
recipes.summary: The great Catalan sauce — a smoky, brick-red emulsion of charred peppers, toasted almonds, and sun-dried tomato, thickened by pounded bread and brightened by a jolt of sherry vinegar, tasting of fire and earth in equal measure.
recipes.description: The great Catalan sauce — a smoky, brick-red emulsion of charred peppers, toasted almonds, and sun-dried tomato, thickened by pounded bread and brightened by a jolt of sherry vinegar, tasting of fire and earth in equal measure.

ingredients.name: Day-old sourdough bread, crusts removed (use GF bread to keep GF)

steps.instruction: Char the bell peppers directly over a gas flame or under a screaming-hot broiler, turning with tongs until completely blackened on all sides — this takes 10–15 minutes. Place in a sealed bag or covered bowl for 15 minutes to steam. Peel off the charred skin (a little residue adds flavor), remove the seeds and core. Wrap the garlic cloves unpeeled in foil with a drizzle of oil and roast at 200 C for 20 minutes until completely soft. Squeeze from skins.

In a dry skillet over medium heat, toast the almonds for 4–6 minutes, tossing frequently, until golden-brown and fragrant. Set aside. In the same pan with a splash of oil, fry the torn bread pieces until golden and crisp on all sides, 3–4 minutes. The toasted bread is the thickener — it emulsifies the sauce and gives it body.

In a food processor or blender, pulse the almonds and toasted bread first until coarsely ground. Add the roasted peppers, garlic, sun-dried tomatoes, smoked paprika, cayenne, sherry vinegar, and salt. Process until a rough, textured paste forms. With the motor running, drizzle in the olive oil to emulsify. Process to your preferred consistency — classic romesco is chunky, not smooth. Taste and adjust: more vinegar for acidity, more paprika for smoke, more oil for richness. The sauce should taste bold enough to be slightly overwhelming on its own.

recipes.title: Scandinavian Rye Bread
recipes.summary: A dense, dark, tangy loaf of rye flour, whole grains, and seeds, long-fermented with a sourdough rye starter into a moist, sliceable crumb that keeps for weeks.
recipes.description: A dense, dark, tangy loaf of rye flour, whole grains, and seeds, long-fermented with a sourdough rye starter into a moist, sliceable crumb that keeps for weeks.

ingredients.name: Cracked rye or rye berries (soaked 12 hr)

steps.instruction: Cover the cracked rye berries or whole rye berries with cold water and leave to soak for 12 hours or overnight. They will absorb a significant amount of water and soften considerably. Drain before using. This soaker adds texture, moisture, and a nutty chew to the finished loaf — unsoaked grains would be unpleasantly hard and would steal hydration from the dough itself during baking.

Combine all the flours, the rye starter, remaining water (adjust for grain moisture), salt, and molasses in a large bowl. Mix vigorously with a wooden spoon or dough scraper — rye dough contains almost no gluten and behaves more like thick batter than bread dough. No kneading is needed or useful: rye proteins do not form gluten strands. Fold in the drained soaker, sunflower seeds, and caraway seeds until evenly distributed. The dough will be very sticky and stiff-heavy — it should hold its shape when scooped but not stretch. Cover and ferment at room temperature 8–12 hours.

Transfer the dough to a well-oiled 9 × 5-inch loaf tin. Dip your hands or a spatula in water and smooth the top into an even dome — rye dough cannot be shaped in the traditional sense; the tin does all the work. Sprinkle a few extra sunflower seeds or caraway on the surface. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and proof at room temperature until the dome crowns about 1 cm above the tin rim and cracks appear in the surface, 2–4 hours. Rye dough will not achieve the dramatic rise of wheat bread — a 20–30% increase is ideal. Preheat the oven to 425°F / 220°C.

Bake at 425°F / 220°C for 15 minutes, then reduce to 375°F / 190°C and bake a further 45–55 minutes. The internal temperature should reach 205°F / 96°C. The loaf will shrink slightly from the tin sides when done. Turn out and cool completely on a wire rack — at least 8 hours, preferably 24 hours — before slicing. The crumb is gummy and unset when hot; slicing too soon produces a sticky, undercooked interior regardless of the actual bake level. The loaf's interior continues to set as it cools.

recipes.title: Salsa Macha
recipes.summary: Oaxaca's oil-based chile-nut condiment — dried árbol and mulato chiles bloomed in hot oil with toasted pumpkin seeds, peanuts, and garlic until the oil itself becomes an aromatic, rust-red medium carrying smoky, nutty, slow-building heat. More oil than sauce, more condiment than salsa, entirely irreplaceable.
recipes.description: Oaxaca's oil-based chile-nut condiment — dried árbol and mulato chiles bloomed in hot oil with toasted pumpkin seeds, peanuts, and garlic until the oil itself becomes an aromatic, rust-red medium carrying smoky, nutty, slow-building heat. More oil than sauce, more condiment than salsa, entirely irreplaceable.

ingredients.name: Dried chiles de árbol (stemmed, seeded or not)
Dried mulato or ancho chile (stemmed, seeded, torn)

steps.instruction: In a dry skillet over medium heat, toast the pepitas and peanuts separately, each stirring constantly. Pepitas first: 3 to 4 minutes until they inflate, turn golden-green, and begin to pop. Remove. Peanuts: 4 to 5 minutes, stirring constantly, until they smell of roasted peanuts and turn a uniform golden-brown. Remove. Do not mix them during toasting — they finish at different times. Cool both completely. The dry-toasting before the oil fry builds a layer of nutty flavor that the oil alone cannot achieve.

In a small saucepan, heat the oil over medium heat. When a piece of garlic dropped in sizzles immediately, add all the garlic slices and fry 60 to 90 seconds until golden — do not let them darken further. Remove garlic with a slotted spoon to a blender. Reduce the oil to medium-low and add both types of dried chiles. They should sizzle gently, not violently. Stir and press them into the oil for 30 to 60 seconds until they turn a darker shade and the oil takes on a deep red color and smells of bloomed dried chile. Watch carefully — dried chiles burn in seconds. Remove chiles immediately with a spider to the blender with the garlic. Reserve the now red-tinged oil.

To the blender with the fried garlic and chiles, add the toasted pepitas and peanuts, vinegar, salt, and sugar (if using). Pour in the reserved red chile oil. Pulse 8 to 12 times — the goal is a very coarse texture, not a smooth puree. Each pulse should break down the nuts and chiles further without turning the whole thing into a paste. The finished salsa macha should have visible nut and chile fragments in a red oil — it is an oil-based condiment, not a thick paste. Taste and adjust salt, vinegar, and sugar. Pour into a jar and seal. The oil and solids will separate on standing — stir or shake before each use.

recipes.title: Salsa Verde Cruda
recipes.summary: The raw Mexican green salsa — tomatillos, jalapeño, onion, and cilantro blended entirely without heat, yielding a grassy, bracingly tart sauce with a crunch of freshness that cooked versions cannot touch. The verde in every taquería worth visiting.
recipes.description: The raw Mexican green salsa — tomatillos, jalapeño, onion, and cilantro blended entirely without heat, yielding a grassy, bracingly tart sauce with a crunch of freshness that cooked versions cannot touch. The verde in every taquería worth visiting.

steps.instruction: Remove the papery husks from the tomatillos and rinse them under cold water, rubbing off the sticky, slightly waxy coating on their skin. This coating is mildly bitter and slightly acidic — removing it ensures the salsa doesn't carry an unwanted soapy note. Quarter them. Taste a small piece raw: the tomatillo should taste bracingly sour with a fruity, apple-like undertone. If they taste flat, they are under-ripe; very ripe tomatillos are better for cooked salsa.

Combine the tomatillos, jalapeño, onion, garlic, cilantro, lime juice, and salt in a blender. Pulse 8 to 12 times — do not blend continuously. The texture should remain slightly chunky, not pureed. Cruda means raw and it means textured. Taste after the first few pulses and adjust: more jalapeño for heat, more lime for brightness, more cilantro for green flavor. The salsa will seem thin but will thicken as it rests.

recipes.title: Salsa Verde (Tomatillo)
recipes.summary: A bright, tangy table sauce from Central Mexico — husked tomatillos and jalapeños blistered under a broiler until their skins blacken and char, then blitzed with raw onion, garlic, and a fistful of cilantro into something vivid and alive. The char is not a mistake; it is the sauce.
recipes.description: A bright, tangy table sauce from Central Mexico — husked tomatillos and jalapeños blistered under a broiler until their skins blacken and char, then blitzed with raw onion, garlic, and a fistful of cilantro into something vivid and alive. The char is not a mistake; it is the sauce.

steps.instruction: Position an oven rack 4 inches beneath the broiler and set it to high. Arrange the tomatillos, whole jalapeños, onion quarters, and unpeeled garlic cloves on a foil-lined baking sheet in a single layer. Broil for 8-10 minutes, rotating the pan once, until the tomatillos are blackened and blistered in spots, softened and collapsing, and the jalapeño skins are charred. Flip everything once at the halfway mark. The garlic should be soft inside its skin.

Squeeze the roasted garlic from its papery skins directly into a blender. Add the charred tomatillos and their accumulated juices, the jalapeños (seeds and all for full heat, or deseed for milder), and the onion. Pulse 4-5 times to break it down, then add the cilantro, lime juice, and salt. Blend to your preferred texture — a few more pulses for rustic and chunky, a 20-second blitz for a pourable sauce.

Taste the salsa and season in layers: add salt first until the tomatillo flavor snaps into focus, then add lime juice in small increments to amplify the brightness without pushing it into sourness. A good salsa verde should taste bright and tangy, with the heat arriving at the back of the palate. Let it rest at room temperature for 10 minutes before serving — the flavors knit together as it sits.

recipes.title: Salsa Verde
recipes.summary: Bright, tangy tomatillos charred under the broiler with serrano chiles and white onion, then blended raw into a salsa that tastes like green fire — acidic, herbaceous, and dangerously drinkable.
recipes.description: Bright, tangy tomatillos charred under the broiler with serrano chiles and white onion, then blended raw into a salsa that tastes like green fire — acidic, herbaceous, and dangerously drinkable.

steps.instruction: Set the oven to broil on high and position a rack 6 inches from the element. Spread the tomatillos (halved if very large), serrano chiles, onion quarters, and unpeeled garlic on a foil-lined baking sheet in a single layer. Broil for 5–6 minutes until the tops are spotted black and blistered. Flip everything with tongs and broil for another 3–4 minutes. The tomatillos should be collapsing and oozing their sticky green juice.

Peel the roasted garlic and transfer all roasted vegetables and their accumulated juices into a blender. Add the cilantro, salt, and lime juice. Pulse 4–5 times for a rough texture, or blend for 30–45 seconds for a smoother sauce. Do not over-blend — some texture is traditional and desirable. Taste immediately and adjust salt and lime.

Taste the salsa critically. Add salt in small increments (a pinch at a time), stirring and tasting between each addition, until the tomatillo flavor pops and the salsa tastes bright rather than dull. A properly salted salsa verde should make you immediately want another taste. Add more lime juice if the acidity has faded. Let rest at room temperature for 10 minutes before serving to allow the flavors to settle.

recipes.title: Sambal Oelek
recipes.summary: Indonesia's foundational raw chili paste — fresh red chilies, salt, and a splash of vinegar pounded in a mortar into a coarse, fiery paste whose pure chili heat and fruity freshness serve as the base of countless Indonesian dishes and the perfect condiment for everything else.
recipes.description: Indonesia's foundational raw chili paste — fresh red chilies, salt, and a splash of vinegar pounded in a mortar into a coarse, fiery paste whose pure chili heat and fruity freshness serve as the base of countless Indonesian dishes and the perfect condiment for everything else.

ingredients.name: Fresh red Fresno or Holland chilies (medium heat), stems removed
Fresh red bird's-eye chilies (cabe rawit), for heat boost (optional)
White vinegar or distilled cane vinegar

steps.instruction: Roughly chop the Fresno chilies into large pieces — halve them lengthwise and cut into thirds. If you prefer a milder sambal, scrape out the seeds and white ribs with a spoon; for full heat, leave them in. If using bird's-eye chilies, leave them whole or halve them. Peel the garlic cloves. This rough prep is all that is needed before the mortar does its work — do not fine-mince. Keep seeds and juice from the cutting board; they are flavour.

Transfer the chopped chilies and garlic to a large granite or stone mortar. Add the salt — salt acts as an abrasive grit that helps break down the fibers faster. Pound with firm, deliberate downward strokes: the pestle should thud, not grind. Begin with harder downward blows to break down the larger pieces, then shift to a rotating, pressing grind for the final paste. The goal is a coarse, rustic paste with visible flecks of chili skin and seeds — not a smooth purée. Sambal oelek's character is its roughness; a blender makes it too uniform and drives off the fresh aroma. Pound for 3–4 minutes total.

Pour the vinegar over the pounded paste and stir to combine. Taste carefully — it should be fiercely hot, brightly acidic, and cleanly salty, with the fresh, fruity aroma of raw chili dominant. Adjust: more salt for presence, more vinegar for brightness and preservation, more garlic pounded in for depth. Transfer to a clean glass jar and press the surface down to eliminate air pockets. Refrigerate. The sambal keeps for up to 2 weeks refrigerated — the vinegar and salt are natural preservatives. The colour will darken slightly from bright scarlet to a deeper red over the first 24 hours as it rests.

recipes.title: Shanghai Scallion Oil Noodles (Cong You Ban Mian)
recipes.summary: Plain wheat noodles tossed in a dark, slow-rendered scallion oil that takes forty minutes to build from a bundle of green onions and a cup of oil — the scallions caramelize to a dark, sweet, crispy confetti while the oil absorbs their entire life force, becoming something wholly different from any oil you have ever tasted. A dish of four ingredients that insists on quality in each one.
recipes.description: Plain wheat noodles tossed in a dark, slow-rendered scallion oil that takes forty minutes to build from a bundle of green onions and a cup of oil — the scallions caramelize to a dark, sweet, crispy confetti while the oil absorbs their entire life force, becoming something wholly different from any oil you have ever tasted. A dish of four ingredients that insists on quality in each one.

ingredients.name: Fresh thin Shanghai noodles (or dried lo mein)

steps.instruction: Combine the scallion pieces and neutral oil in a cold small saucepan or wok — starting in cold oil is critical. If you add scallions to already-hot oil they will fry hard and fast, browning too quickly before they have time to release their aromatics into the oil. Place over the lowest heat you can manage and cook for 30–40 minutes. The first 15 minutes will see very little activity — the oil will warm slowly and the scallions will begin to soften and wilt. From 15–25 minutes, the scallions will begin to shrink dramatically and you will see the first signs of browning at the green tips. From 25–40 minutes, the scallions will caramelize progressively from the tips down toward the white roots, going from golden to amber to a deep reddish-brown. The goal is that the scallions go almost fully dark — sweet-bitter, crispy shards — while the oil turns a deep golden-amber and smells like nothing else: sweet, savory, deeply caramelized allium. Stir every 5 minutes, more frequently in the last 10. When the scallion pieces are uniformly dark golden-brown and crispy, remove from heat.

In a large mixing bowl that will also serve as your tossing bowl for the noodles, combine the warm scallion oil (about 3 tablespoons per serving), light soy sauce, dark soy sauce, and sugar. Stir together with a spoon or chopsticks until the sugar is fully dissolved. The sauce will be a dark, glossy, highly aromatic liquid — the dark soy provides color and depth, the light soy provides salinity and brightness. Taste it: it should be very salty and intensely sweet-savory, because it will dilute dramatically when tossed with the starchy noodles. The ratio of scallion oil to soy sauce is important: too much oil and the noodles are greasy; too much soy and they are one-dimensionally salty. Adjust to your preference — more dark soy for a deeper color and molasses-sweet flavor, more light soy for a brighter, saltier result.

Cook the noodles in a large pot of vigorously boiling, lightly salted water until just done — fresh Shanghai noodles take 2–3 minutes, dried lo mein 4–5 minutes, thin spaghetti 7–8 minutes. Drain well, shaking the colander hard. Transfer immediately to the bowl of scallion sauce while the noodles are still very hot — the heat helps the sauce coat every strand. Toss vigorously and quickly with chopsticks or tongs, lifting and folding the noodles continuously for 60–90 seconds until every strand is evenly coated in the dark, glossy sauce. The hot noodles will absorb the soy quickly, so work fast. Taste and adjust: more soy for salt, more oil for richness, a few drops of scallion oil for aroma. Transfer to a serving plate or bowl and scatter a generous amount of the reserved crispy scallion pieces over the top. Serve immediately — scallion oil noodles are a dish of the moment, and the texture deteriorates rapidly.

recipes.title: Scallion Oil
recipes.summary: Shanghai's most versatile condiment — neutral oil slowly infused with ginger and a mountain of scallions until they turn golden and fragrant, leaving behind an oil that elevates everything it touches.
recipes.description: Shanghai's most versatile condiment — neutral oil slowly infused with ginger and a mountain of scallions until they turn golden and fragrant, leaving behind an oil that elevates everything it touches.

ingredients.name: Fresh ginger, peeled and sliced 5 mm thick

steps.instruction: Trim and wash the scallions thoroughly — any trapped moisture will cause the oil to splatter aggressively when they hit the pan. Pat completely dry with paper towels, or better, lay them out for 30 minutes to air-dry. Combine the oil, whole scallions, and ginger slices in a cold wok or medium saucepan. Place over medium-low heat. Starting cold is essential — it gives the scallion and ginger time to slowly release their volatile aromatic compounds into the oil before any browning occurs. As the oil heats, the scallions will begin to wilt, then soften, then bubble. The bubbling is the water content of the scallion cooking off — as long as it is bubbling vigorously, the temperature will stay below browning. Let the oil slowly infuse for 10–12 minutes, turning the scallions occasionally with tongs.

After the initial infusion, increase the heat to medium and allow the oil to continue cooking the scallions until they transition from jade-green to a pale golden-yellow, with the edges beginning to show the first signs of browning. This stage takes 5–8 minutes after the heat is raised. Watch for the moment the vigorous bubbling slows — this means the scallions have lost most of their moisture and are now beginning to actually fry in the oil rather than steam. This is when browning accelerates rapidly. As soon as the scallions are golden-yellow with pale amber tips, remove from heat — they will continue to cook in the residual heat of the oil.

Remove the pan from the heat and immediately stir in the salt — it will dissolve into the hot oil and season it throughout. Let the oil cool slightly for 2–3 minutes (the scallions will continue to cook in the residual heat, deepening slightly from golden to pale amber). Then strain the oil through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean heat-proof jar or container, pressing gently on the solids to extract every drop of flavored oil. Discard the spent scallion and ginger solids — they have given everything to the oil and have nothing left to offer. Let the oil cool to room temperature before sealing. It keeps refrigerated for up to 3 weeks and solidifies slightly when cold; bring to room temperature before using. Drizzle over cold noodles, steamed fish, congee, or use anywhere the gentle, sweet fragrance of scallion should be present without the texture of raw scallion.

recipes.title: Schiacciata
recipes.summary: Tuscany's answer to focaccia — thinner, crispier at the edges, and so saturated with good olive oil that the first bite releases a warm, grassy flood — the word 'schiacciata' means crushed, and the flat, dimpled dough delivers exactly that: deliberately pressed-down, maximally crisp.
recipes.description: Tuscany's answer to focaccia — thinner, crispier at the edges, and so saturated with good olive oil that the first bite releases a warm, grassy flood — the word 'schiacciata' means crushed, and the flat, dimpled dough delivers exactly that: deliberately pressed-down, maximally crisp.

ingredients.name: Extra-virgin olive oil, plus generous amount for pan and top
Flaky sea salt (Maldon or Fiore di Sale)

steps.instruction: Combine the flour, instant yeast, and fine salt in a large bowl, keeping the salt and yeast on opposite sides of the bowl initially. Pour in the warm water and olive oil. Mix with a dough scraper or your hand until no dry flour remains — the dough will be moderately sticky, softer than a bread dough but not as wet as focaccia. It should pull away from the sides of the bowl. Do not add more flour. Cover and rest for 15 minutes.

Perform three sets of stretch-and-fold over 60 minutes, one set every 20 minutes. For each set: wet your hand, grab the dough at one side of the bowl, stretch it firmly upward as far as it will reach without tearing, then fold it over the center. Rotate the bowl 90 degrees and repeat until you have completed four folds. After three sets, the dough should be noticeably smoother, more cohesive, and beginning to show bubbles beneath the surface. Cover and let bulk ferment at room temperature for another 30 minutes until puffy.

Pour a very generous amount of olive oil onto a half-sheet pan or rimmed baking tray — at least 4-5 tablespoons. Schiacciata is an olive oil bread and should practically float in it. Transfer the dough to the pan and use your fingertips to begin pressing and stretching it toward the edges. If the dough springs back firmly, cover and wait 10-15 minutes, then try again. The dough should eventually be pressed quite flat — roughly 1.5 cm thick throughout. Cover with plastic wrap and proof at room temperature for 30-45 minutes until noticeably puffy and slightly domed.

Using all ten fingers held flat, press the dough firmly and repeatedly across its entire surface, pushing all the way through to the pan. The dough should be pressed quite flat — flatter than focaccia. This is the 'schiacciata' — the crushing. Drizzle another generous pour of olive oil across the entire surface, letting it pool in the dimples. Scatter the flaky salt and rosemary leaves if using. The salt goes on now, not after baking.

Bake at 230 C (450 F) on the lowest rack for 15-20 minutes. Schiacciata bakes hotter and faster than focaccia because it is thinner. Watch carefully after 12 minutes. The edges should be deep brown and very crisp; the center should be golden. Remove from the pan immediately to a wire rack — do not let it cool in the pan or the bottom will steam and soften. Cool for 5 minutes before cutting. Schiacciata is best eaten within 1 hour of baking, while the contrast between the crisp exterior and the moist, oily crumb is still at its peak.

recipes.title: Socca Niçoise
recipes.summary: Nice's beloved street pancake: a thin, caramel-spotted disc of chickpea flour batter cooked in a blazing iron pan until the edges shatter and the center stays yielding, then torn apart at the table and eaten with fingers dusted in black pepper.
recipes.description: Nice's beloved street pancake: a thin, caramel-spotted disc of chickpea flour batter cooked in a blazing iron pan until the edges shatter and the center stays yielding, then torn apart at the table and eaten with fingers dusted in black pepper.

ingredients.name: Extra-virgin olive oil (plus more for the pan)

steps.instruction: Place chickpea flour in a bowl. Slowly pour the cold water over it while whisking — always add water to flour, not flour to water, to prevent lumps. Whisk until completely smooth, then add olive oil and salt. Whisk again. The batter should be thinner than pancake batter — nearly as thin as whole milk. Skim off any foam. Rest uncovered at room temperature for 1 hour minimum. The rest allows the flour to hydrate fully and the batter to develop a creamy, nutty character.

Place a 30–32 cm cast-iron skillet or a round carbon-steel pan under the broiler set to maximum. After 10 minutes, use thick oven gloves to remove the screaming-hot pan. Pour in 2 tbsp olive oil, swirl to coat, then quickly pour in enough batter to cover the surface to 4–5 mm depth. Return immediately to the broiler. Broil 6–8 minutes until the top is blistered and golden-brown in patches and the edges are dark and crisp. Scatter cracked pepper over the top in the last 2 minutes. The center will remain slightly soft — this is correct.

recipes.title: Sourdough Boule
recipes.summary: A high-hydration country loaf born of wild yeast and patience — its crust shatters like porcelain, its crumb opens in dramatic, irregular caves that catch butter and hold jam. This is the Pacific Northwest's daily bread: naturally leavened, deeply flavored, unapologetically sour.
recipes.description: A high-hydration country loaf born of wild yeast and patience — its crust shatters like porcelain, its crumb opens in dramatic, irregular caves that catch butter and hold jam. This is the Pacific Northwest's daily bread: naturally leavened, deeply flavored, unapologetically sour.

steps.instruction: Combine flour and water in a large bowl. Mix by hand until no dry flour remains — this takes about 2 minutes of rough mixing. The dough will be shaggy and rough, almost reluctant. Cover and rest at room temperature for 30–60 minutes. During this rest, the flour's enzymes begin breaking down proteins and starch, and gluten bonds form without any mechanical effort. When you return to the dough, it will have visibly smoothed and relaxed.

Add the active starter and scatter the salt over the dough surface. Dimple the salt in with your fingers, then perform a series of 4 stretch-and-folds: wet your hand, reach under one side of the dough, stretch it up until you feel resistance, then fold it over the top. Rotate the bowl 90° and repeat all the way around. Do this for 4 rounds total, spaced 30 minutes apart. After the last fold, let the dough bulk ferment undisturbed at 75–78°F (24–26°C) for a total of 4–5 hours from when starter was added, until it has grown by 50–75% and is visibly bubbly throughout.

Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface. Fold the edges in toward the center, then flip it seam-side down. Using both hands cupped around the dough, drag it toward you across the bench with gentle downward pressure — the friction tightens the surface. Repeat this motion 4–5 times, rotating slightly each pass, until the boule has a taut, smooth top with no tears. Transfer seam-side up into a well-floured banneton (rice flour is ideal) or a flour-dusted bowl lined with a floured tea towel. The boule should hold a round shape and not sag sideways.

Refrigerate the shaped boule, covered, for 10–16 hours (overnight is ideal). The cold retard slows fermentation while allowing the sour flavor to develop and the dough to firm up for cleaner scoring. The dough does not need to look dramatically different after retarding — a slight increase in size is normal. Bake directly from the refrigerator without warming to room temperature; the cold dough will score more cleanly.

Place a Dutch oven in the oven and preheat to 500°F (260°C) for at least 45 minutes. When oven-hot, remove the boule from the refrigerator. Cut a large square of parchment to act as a sling. Flip the cold boule seam-side down onto the parchment. Using a lame or sharp bread knife held at a 30–45° angle, score a single confident arc across the top — the ear — with one continuous stroke. Depth should be about ½ inch (1.2 cm). Additional decorative scores can be added perpendicular, but the main ear is the pressure valve.

Lower the boule on its parchment into the preheated Dutch oven. Cover with the lid and bake at 500°F for 20 minutes (the steam from the dough creates the oven-spring environment). Remove the lid, drop the temperature to 460°F (238°C), and bake a further 20–25 minutes uncovered until the crust is a deep mahogany-brown. Remove from the Dutch oven and cool on a wire rack for at least 1 hour before cutting — the crumb is still setting up inside.

recipes.title: Sourdough Country Loaf
recipes.summary: A naturally leavened open-crumb loaf built from active starter, high-hydration dough, cold retard overnight, and baked in a Dutch oven until the crust shatters and the interior glistens.
recipes.description: A naturally leavened open-crumb loaf built from active starter, high-hydration dough, cold retard overnight, and baked in a Dutch oven until the crust shatters and the interior glistens.

steps.instruction: Combine the bread flour and whole wheat flour in a large bowl. Pour in the water (holding back about 30 g for the salt later) and mix with your hand until no dry flour remains — squeeze and fold until the mass is shaggy and fully hydrated. Cover and rest 30–60 minutes at room temperature. The autolyse lets enzymes begin degrading the starches and the gluten proteins hydrate and loosely align without mechanical work, making subsequent mixing far more efficient and giving the crumb a silkier extensibility.

Dissolve the salt in the reserved water, then pour starter and salt water over the autolysed dough. Use the pinch-and-fold method: pinch the starter through the dough in 10–15 passes until integrated. Then begin the series of stretch-and-folds: every 30 minutes for the first 2 hours, grab one edge of the dough, stretch it up until you feel resistance, and fold it to the opposite side. Rotate the bowl 90° and repeat four times per set. After four sets, leave the dough covered to finish bulk fermentation — roughly 10–14 hours at 68°F / 20°C, or 4–5 hours at 76°F / 24°C. The dough is ready when it has grown by 50–75%, feels airy and domed, and a flap peeled back shows a network of bubbles just below the surface.

Turn the dough gently onto an unfloured surface. Using a bench scraper and one cupped hand, do a pre-shape: drag the dough toward you while the scraper pushes from behind, rotating to build surface tension into a loose round. Rest uncovered 20–30 minutes (bench rest). Then flour the top of the round generously, flip it, and do the final shape: for a boule, grab the far edge, fold it to the center, then fold left, right, and roll the whole package toward you, using your palms to drag and seal the bottom seam tight against the bench. The surface should be taut like a drum. Drop seam-side-up into a well-floured (rice flour is ideal) banneton or a bowl lined with a floured towel. Pinch the seam closed. Cover and refrigerate 12–16 hours.

Preheat the oven with a Dutch oven (lid on) inside to 500°F / 260°C for at least 45 minutes. Turn the cold loaf out of the banneton onto a piece of parchment. Working fast, score with a lame or sharp razor blade held at a 30–45° angle: a single ear cut down one side of the dome, or a bold cross-hatch. The cut should be decisive and swift — 5–7 cm deep — not a timid scratch. The cold dough (straight from the fridge) is easiest to score cleanly.

Using the parchment as a sling, lower the loaf into the screaming-hot Dutch oven and put the lid on. Bake covered at 500°F / 260°C for 20 minutes — steam from the dough trapped inside the pot creates the glossy, extensible crust needed for maximum oven spring. Remove the lid, drop the temperature to 460°F / 238°C, and bake a further 20–25 minutes until the crust is deep mahogany and an instant-read thermometer at the center reads 205–210°F / 96–99°C. Transfer to a wire rack and resist cutting for at least 1 hour — the interior crumb is still setting via residual heat.

recipes.title: Sourdough Starter
recipes.summary: A living culture built from nothing but flour and water — coaxed over a week from a flat, lifeless slurry into a billowing, sweet-sour leaven that doubles on schedule and smells of ripe yogurt and green apple. Feed it, watch it breathe, and it will raise bread for a lifetime.
recipes.description: A living culture built from nothing but flour and water — coaxed over a week from a flat, lifeless slurry into a billowing, sweet-sour leaven that doubles on schedule and smells of ripe yogurt and green apple. Feed it, watch it breathe, and it will raise bread for a lifetime.

ingredients.name: Whole rye flour (for the first build — high in wild yeast and enzymes)
Unbleached bread or all-purpose flour (for daily feeds)
Mature starter discard (carried forward at each feed)

steps.instruction: In a clean glass jar, stir the whole rye flour and warm water into a thick, lump-free paste — the consistency of pancake batter. Scrape down the sides, mark the level with a rubber band or tape, and cover loosely so gas can escape but the surface stays protected. Rest at warm room temperature, 24–26°C, for 24 hours. Rye carries a dense population of wild yeast and lactic bacteria plus the enzymes that feed them, so it kick-starts a culture faster than white flour ever could.

Begin daily feeds. Discard all but about 50 g of the slurry, then stir in equal weights of fresh flour and warm water — roughly 50 g each. Switch to unbleached bread or all-purpose flour now; it builds the gluten strength you want in a leaven. Re-mark the level, cover loosely, and keep warm. Feed once every 24 hours for days 3 and 4. Discarding keeps the culture young and the acid low enough for the yeast to multiply; without it the mixture turns too sour for the yeast to thrive.

From around day 5, feed twice daily, every 12 hours, discarding to ~50 g each time and refreshing with equal flour and water. The culture should now be reliable: rising and falling on a predictable rhythm. Watch one full cycle from feed to peak — when it consistently doubles within 4–8 hours and smells sweet-sour and ripe, it is mature. Confirm readiness with the float test: drop a spoonful of peaked starter into water. If it floats, it is buoyant with gas and ready to leaven bread.

To keep the starter alive long-term, settle into a maintenance feed: carry forward 50 g of mature starter, discard the rest, and refresh with 50 g flour and 50 g water (a 1:1:1 ratio). If baking often, hold it at room temperature and feed once or twice daily. If baking occasionally, store it in the fridge and feed weekly — let it warm and rise once at room temperature before each bake. A well-kept starter improves for years, deepening in flavor and reliability.

recipes.title: South Indian Idli Batter
recipes.summary: Parboiled rice and split black lentils, soaked separately and ground to a silky batter, then left overnight to ferment until airy and slightly sour — the foundation of idli, dosa, and uttapam across South India.
recipes.description: Parboiled rice and split black lentils, soaked separately and ground to a silky batter, then left overnight to ferment until airy and slightly sour — the foundation of idli, dosa, and uttapam across South India.

steps.instruction: Rinse the rice 3-4 times until the water runs clear. Rinse the urad dal and fenugreek seeds together 2-3 times. Soak them in separate bowls of cold water for 6-8 hours (or overnight). Keep the bowls in a cool spot — not refrigerated. The soaking water should cover the grains by at least 5cm as they will swell significantly. The fenugreek seeds soak with the urad dal. After soaking, drain each bowl but reserve the urad dal soaking water separately — it contains wild yeasts and bacteria that help fermentation.

Grind the urad dal and fenugreek seeds first in a wet grinder or high-powered blender with the reserved soaking water (or cold water), adding water tablespoon by tablespoon. Grind for 20-30 minutes in a wet grinder (or 5-10 minutes in a high-speed blender) until the batter is completely smooth, extremely fine, and very fluffy — it should have a whipped, airy quality from the air incorporation during grinding. The traditional wet grinder stone generates minimal heat and grinds ultra-fine. Transfer to a large bowl. Then grind the soaked rice with cold water until smooth but slightly grainy — just a bit of texture is desirable in idli rice batter. Combine both batters and mix well.

Stir the salt into the combined batter thoroughly — salt helps control unwanted bacteria during fermentation. The batter should be of a consistency that falls off a spoon in a thick ribbon. Transfer to a large container (the batter will roughly double in volume during fermentation — the container must be large enough). Cover loosely with a lid or cloth. Leave in a warm place — 28-32°C (82-90°F) is ideal. In Indian summer climates this happens overnight (8-12 hours). In cooler climates it may take 16-24 hours. The oven with only the light on (around 27°C) works well in cool kitchens. Fermentation is complete when the batter has risen significantly, looks fluffy and aerated, has a pleasant sour smell, and tiny bubbles are visible throughout.

Grease the idli molds lightly with oil. Gently stir the batter from the bottom without deflating it too much. Ladle batter into each mold, filling about three-quarters full — they will expand during steaming. Steam over vigorously boiling water for 10-12 minutes. Do not lift the lid during steaming. The idli are done when a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean and the surface is set and slightly dry. Unmold immediately after 2 minutes of cooling by running a wet spoon around each idli. They should pop out cleanly.

recipes.title: Sticky Rice (Khao Niao)
recipes.summary: Northern Thailand's staple glutinous rice — soaked overnight and steamed in a bamboo basket over a clay pot of boiling water until the grains turn translucent and sticky, perfect for rolling into balls and dipping into everything.
recipes.description: Northern Thailand's staple glutinous rice — soaked overnight and steamed in a bamboo basket over a clay pot of boiling water until the grains turn translucent and sticky, perfect for rolling into balls and dipping into everything.

ingredients.name: Boiling water, for steaming (in pot below)

steps.instruction: Rinse the glutinous rice under cold running water, swirling with your hand, until the water runs mostly clear — this removes excess surface starch that would otherwise make the cooked rice gummy rather than sticky. Transfer to a large bowl and cover with cold water by at least 5 cm. Soak for a minimum of 4 hours; overnight (8–12 hours) is strongly preferred. The grains must be fully hydrated before steaming — without this soak, the interior of each grain will remain hard and chalky no matter how long you steam them. The rice is ready to drain when each grain has swollen, turned chalky-white all the way through, and feels soft when pressed between two fingers but does not shatter.

Pour the boiling water into a wide clay pot, wok, or large saucepan — whichever will fit your bamboo steaming basket (or a heatproof colander lined with muslin). The water should be deep enough that it does not touch the bottom of the basket, but not so high that you have to refill frequently. Bring it to a full, rolling boil before loading the rice. Line the bamboo basket with a single layer of damp cheesecloth or muslin to prevent rice from falling through the slats.

Spread the drained glutinous rice evenly in the lined bamboo basket in a layer no thicker than 4 cm. Cover and steam over the vigorously boiling water for 12 minutes. The heat will gelatinize the outer layers of starch first. After 12 minutes, flip the rice mass over using the cloth liner — this is the key step that ensures even cooking from both surfaces. The bottom layer will already look glossy and slightly translucent; the top will still look chalky. After flipping, level the mass and continue steaming for another 8–10 minutes.

After a total of 20–22 minutes steaming (12 minutes + 8–10 minutes after flip), remove the basket from the pot. Taste a few grains from the center of the mass — they should be uniformly tender, sticky, and slightly sweet with no chalky or hard core. Turn the rice out of the cloth into a traditional sticky-rice serving basket (a krathip) or a covered bowl lined with a clean cloth to keep it warm and prevent it from drying out. Do not leave it exposed to air — it stiffens within minutes. Sticky rice is eaten by hand: pinch a small amount and roll it into a ball with your fingers, using the warm, malleable texture of the rice itself as the adhesive.

recipes.title: İmam Bayıldı (Stuffed Eggplant)
recipes.summary: Slender eggplants scored and salted, then lavishly filled with sweet onion, garlic, and ripe tomato cooked down in pools of olive oil — braised until the flesh gives completely and the name's legend proves itself: the imam fainted from pleasure.
recipes.description: Slender eggplants scored and salted, then lavishly filled with sweet onion, garlic, and ripe tomato cooked down in pools of olive oil — braised until the flesh gives completely and the name's legend proves itself: the imam fainted from pleasure.

ingredients.name: Ripe plum tomatoes, peeled and chopped
Fine sea salt and white sugar

steps.instruction: Wash and dry eggplants. Leave the stem on for presentation. Make a deep lengthwise slit in each eggplant from tip to within 2 cm of the stem, cutting three-quarters of the way through — creating a pocket. Rub the interior of the slit generously with fine salt. Place slit-side down in a colander for 30 minutes to draw out excess moisture and any bitterness.

Heat half the olive oil in a wide pan over medium. Add onion slices and a large pinch of salt and the sugar. Cook slowly, stirring every few minutes, for 15 minutes until deeply golden and jammy. Add garlic and cook 3 minutes. Add tomatoes and cook until the mixture is thick, unified, and the oil has separated to the surface — another 8 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in parsley.

Heat remaining olive oil in a wide oven-safe pan or casserole over medium-high. Add eggplants slit-side down and fry for 3–4 minutes until the cut face is golden. Turn carefully and fry the skin side 2–3 minutes. The eggplant should already be beginning to soften. Remove briefly to a board.

Stuff each eggplant generously, opening the slit with fingers and packing in the filling so it mounds above the opening. Arrange stuffed eggplants tightly in a wide, heavy pan or casserole, slit-side up. Pour any remaining filling liquid and the water around (not over) the eggplants. Drizzle the remaining olive oil over the tops. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover, and cook over low heat for 35–45 minutes until the eggplant is completely tender. Cool to room temperature before serving.

recipes.title: Sukuma Wiki
recipes.summary: Collard greens sautéed with tomato, onion, and a whisper of chili — Kenya's everyday green, whose name means 'push the week' in Swahili, a dish cooked in every household from Nairobi to Mombasa, at once humble and deeply satisfying.
recipes.description: Collard greens sautéed with tomato, onion, and a whisper of chili — Kenya's everyday green, whose name means 'push the week' in Swahili, a dish cooked in every household from Nairobi to Mombasa, at once humble and deeply satisfying.

ingredients.name: Collard greens (sukuma wiki) — stems stripped, leaves chiffonade

steps.instruction: Strip the tough central stem from each collard leaf by folding the leaf in half lengthwise and pulling the stem away. Stack several leaves, roll tightly like a cigar, and slice into thin ribbons (chiffonade) about 1cm wide. Thinner slices cook more quickly and evenly — thick slices need much longer cooking and remain tough. Wash in cold water and drain but do not dry completely — the residual water helps the greens steam as they cook.

Heat oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Add the sliced onion and cook for 5–6 minutes until softened and beginning to turn golden. Add the garlic and green chili and cook for 1 minute. Add the tomatoes and cook for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until they break down into a rough sauce. The tomato provides the liquid and acidity that balance the bitterness of the collard greens.

Add the collard green ribbons to the pan all at once — they will seem like too much but will reduce dramatically. Toss aggressively with tongs to coat in the tomato-onion sauce. Season with salt. Add the splash of water and cover the pan for 2 minutes to steam the greens. Uncover, toss again, and cook for 3–5 more minutes over high heat until the greens are fully wilted but still hold a vibrant green color and pleasant bite.

Transfer to a serving dish and serve immediately. Sukuma wiki waits for no one — it loses color and texture with every minute it sits. The traditional accompaniment is ugali (a stiff maize porridge) which absorbs the juices from the greens. A fried egg on the side is the Kenyan working-family's way of making it a full meal.

recipes.title: Lebanese Tabbouleh
recipes.summary: A salad of the finest-chopped flat-leaf parsley with just enough bulgur to catch the lemon juice and olive oil — bright, herb-forward, and electric with acid, meant to be scooped with torn romaine or little gem leaves.
recipes.description: A salad of the finest-chopped flat-leaf parsley with just enough bulgur to catch the lemon juice and olive oil — bright, herb-forward, and electric with acid, meant to be scooped with torn romaine or little gem leaves.

ingredients.name: Scallion or white onion, very finely sliced

steps.instruction: Place the fine bulgur in a small bowl. Pour about half the lemon juice directly over it and stir to wet every grain. Fine bulgur rehydrates entirely without heat — the acid in the lemon juice softens it in 15 minutes while simultaneously seasoning it and reducing its raw, starchy edge. Do not add water. Set aside at room temperature while you prepare the herbs and vegetables. After 15 minutes, squeeze the bulgur in your fist to check that it has softened completely. If still gritty, add another splash of lemon and wait 5 more minutes.

This is the defining technique of tabbouleh: the parsley must be chopped by hand, not in a food processor. A food processor bruises the leaves and releases water that will make the salad wet and dark. Take a large bunch of dry, dry parsley (wash and spin-dry thoroughly beforehand). Gather the leaves tightly and use a sharp heavy knife to rock-chop them into the finest possible mince — almost a dust. The goal is a cloud-light herb mass, not a wet paste. Separately, dice the tomatoes very finely (no larger than 5 mm) and salt them in a colander for 5 minutes, then press out as much juice as possible. Finely chop the mint and slice the scallion paper-thin.

Combine the soaked bulgur, finely chopped parsley, drained tomato, mint, and scallion in a large bowl. Pour the remaining lemon juice over everything, followed by the olive oil. Season with salt and freshly ground black pepper. Toss gently but thoroughly with two large spoons or with clean hands. Taste immediately: tabbouleh should be aggressively bright and acidic — the lemon should be the first and last thing you taste. If it tastes flat or dull, it needs more lemon juice and salt. Adjust until the acid makes your mouth water.

Cover and rest the tabbouleh at room temperature for 10–15 minutes before serving. This short rest allows the bulgur to absorb the last of the dressing, the tomatoes to release a final exchange of juice into the salad, and the mint and scallion flavors to integrate with the parsley. Taste once more before serving and adjust acid and salt a final time. Serve piled on a flat plate surrounded by whole romaine or little gem lettuce leaves for scooping. Tabbouleh does not keep well — serve the day it is made.

recipes.title: Tabouli
recipes.summary: Lebanon's great herb salad — an enormous, verdant mass of flat-leaf parsley and mint, finely hand-chopped, with only a small quantity of fine bulgur soaked (never cooked), dressed aggressively with lemon juice and olive oil; the grain is an accent, the parsley is everything.
