recipes.description: Lebanon's great herb salad — an enormous, verdant mass of flat-leaf parsley and mint, finely hand-chopped, with only a small quantity of fine bulgur soaked (never cooked), dressed aggressively with lemon juice and olive oil; the grain is an accent, the parsley is everything.

ingredients.name: Flat-leaf parsley (4 large bunches, leaves and fine stems only)
Ripe tomatoes (finely diced, drained of excess juice)
Scallions (white and pale green parts, thinly sliced)

steps.instruction: Place the fine bulgur in a small bowl. Pour half the lemon juice (40 ml) directly over it — soaking in lemon juice rather than water means the bulgur absorbs acidity as it hydrates, so it is never bland or watery. Add just enough cold water to barely cover the grain (about 50 ml). Stir once and leave to soak for 20 minutes. After soaking, tip the bulgur into the center of a clean kitchen towel or several layers of cheesecloth and wring firmly — extracting as much liquid as possible. The bulgur must be as dry as you can make it, or it will water down the salad.

Wash and thoroughly dry the parsley and mint — wet herbs will release water into the salad. Use a sharp chef's knife only — never a food processor, which bruises the leaves and turns them dark and bitter within minutes. Gather the parsley into a tight bundle and chop fine with a rocking motion, then rotate 90 degrees and chop again. The goal is a fine, green confetti — not a paste, not rough chunks. Chop the mint separately (it is more delicate) and fold it in. The volume of herb should be approximately 4-5 times the volume of everything else; if you feel you have too much parsley, you are probably correct.

Dice the tomatoes into small cubes, no larger than 5 mm. Place the diced tomatoes in a fine-mesh sieve or colander and let them drain for 10 minutes — tomatoes release a lot of water, and undrained tomatoes will pool at the bottom of the salad within minutes of serving. Slice the scallions into thin rounds. The scallion provides the onion note in tabouli — raw white onion is traditional in some versions, but scallions are milder and more commonly used in modern Lebanese kitchens.

In a large mixing bowl, combine the chopped herbs, squeezed-dry bulgur, drained tomatoes, and scallions. Drizzle the remaining lemon juice and olive oil over everything. Add the allspice, cinnamon, salt, and pepper. Toss gently but thoroughly using two large spoons or clean hands, lifting from the bottom and turning — you are not trying to crush anything, just coat every element in the dressing. The salad will compress slightly as it is tossed. Taste: tabouli should be aggressively, almost bracingly lemony. If it seems too mild, add more lemon juice.

Taste the dressed tabouli and adjust. The correct seasoning for tabouli is different from most dishes: the lemon must be the loudest note — if you are hesitant, add more. The olive oil should be present but should not make the salad heavy. The allspice and cinnamon are subtle warmth, not detectable as distinct spices. Salt should make everything pop without being perceptible on its own. Let the tabouli rest at room temperature for 15 minutes before serving — this brief rest allows the salt to draw a small amount of moisture from the herbs, which mingles with the dressing and creates the finished sauce.

recipes.title: Tahini
recipes.summary: Ground sesame paste — the foundation of hummus, baba ganoush, and a hundred sauces — made by toasting raw sesame seeds at the lowest possible heat until barely golden and blending them long and slow into a smooth, pourable ivory cream. The quality of the tahini determines everything that follows it.
recipes.description: Ground sesame paste — the foundation of hummus, baba ganoush, and a hundred sauces — made by toasting raw sesame seeds at the lowest possible heat until barely golden and blending them long and slow into a smooth, pourable ivory cream. The quality of the tahini determines everything that follows it.

steps.instruction: Spread the raw sesame seeds in a single layer in a wide, dry skillet over medium-low heat. Stir almost constantly with a wooden spoon or shake the pan every 15 to 20 seconds. The seeds will begin to jump and pop as they heat. Your goal is a very light toast — just enough to wake up their nutty flavour and drive off surface moisture, not to colour them. This is a patient, watchful job: sesame goes from perfect to bitter in under 30 seconds. The difference between raw and properly toasted is subtle in colour but significant in flavour.

Tip the toasted sesame seeds onto a cool plate or baking sheet and spread them into a single layer. Let them rest for at least 5 minutes until they reach room temperature. Blending hot sesame seeds carries two risks: the steam they release will condense inside the blender and introduce moisture, which can seize the paste; and the heat can make the blending motor run very hot, shortening its life. Patience here is structural, not optional.

Transfer the cooled seeds to a high-powered blender or food processor. Blend continuously on high for 3 to 4 minutes, scraping down the sides every 60 seconds. The transformation happens in stages: first a coarse, dry crumble; then a thick, clumping ball that rides the blade; then, as the seeds' own oils are released, a sudden collapse into a rough paste; finally, with continued blending, a smooth, flowing cream. If the machine struggles or the paste refuses to loosen after 3 minutes, add the neutral oil one teaspoon at a time, blending after each addition. Do not over-oil — the goal is a paste that moves on its own. Taste and add salt if desired.

recipes.title: Agua de Tamarindo
recipes.summary: The most complex of the aguas frescas — tamarind pods cracked open to reveal their sticky, dark pulp, which is dissolved in hot water and coaxed into a dark amber drink that is profoundly sour, faintly sweet, and loaded with a fruity depth that is halfway between ripe date and tart apricot.
recipes.description: The most complex of the aguas frescas — tamarind pods cracked open to reveal their sticky, dark pulp, which is dissolved in hot water and coaxed into a dark amber drink that is profoundly sour, faintly sweet, and loaded with a fruity depth that is halfway between ripe date and tart apricot.

steps.instruction: If using fresh pods, crack the hard brittle shells and peel them away, pulling off the dark stringy fibres that run lengthwise down the pod. The sticky, chestnut-coloured pulp inside should feel soft and dense. If using a seedless block, simply break it into rough chunks. Place the pulp in a heatproof bowl and pour the boiling water over it. Let it sit for 10 minutes, pressing and massaging the pulp with a fork or your fingers every few minutes — you will feel it loosen and dissolve into the water progressively. The liquid will turn a deep amber-brown.

Set a fine-mesh sieve over a large jug. Pour the tamarind water and pulp into the sieve and press firmly with the back of a large spoon, working in circular motions. The dark amber liquid will pass through while the fibres, seeds, and seed skins remain behind. Keep pressing until the residue in the sieve is nearly dry and fibrous. Discard the solids. The resulting concentrate should be a thick, dark amber liquid with a consistency slightly thicker than water — intensely sour and complex.

Stir the sugar into the warm concentrate until completely dissolved, then add the pinch of salt. Pour in the cold diluting water gradually, tasting as you go — tamarind is assertive and the balance between sour, sweet, and salty is what defines the drink. The final agua should taste powerfully of tamarind fruit first, with the sweetness arriving second and the salt as a distant back note that makes the sourness pop. Refrigerate until cold. Stir before each pour as fine sediment will settle. Serve over ice.

recipes.title: Tamarind-Date Chutney
recipes.summary: The dark, sticky sweet-and-sour chutney of the Indian chaat cart — tamarind pulp simmered with dates, jaggery, and cumin into a glossy, concentrated dip that makes fried things sing.
recipes.description: The dark, sticky sweet-and-sour chutney of the Indian chaat cart — tamarind pulp simmered with dates, jaggery, and cumin into a glossy, concentrated dip that makes fried things sing.

ingredients.name: Tamarind block (seedless pressed pulp), roughly broken
Jaggery or dark muscovado sugar, grated

steps.instruction: Break the tamarind block into rough pieces and submerge in the measured hot water in a bowl. Press the block down with your fingers and leave to soak for 15 minutes, pressing and kneading the pulp every few minutes to help it dissolve. After 15 minutes, the block should have broken down almost entirely. Pour the mixture through a coarse sieve set over a saucepan, pressing firmly with the back of a spoon to extract every drop of the sour brown liquid. Discard the fibrous solids and seeds that remain in the sieve. The resulting tamarind water should taste intensely, bracingly sour — almost mouth-puckering.

Add the chopped dates, grated jaggery, ground cumin, dried ginger, Kashmiri chili powder, fine salt, and kala namak to the tamarind water in the saucepan. Bring to a simmer over medium heat, stirring to dissolve the jaggery. The mixture will foam initially as the jaggery melts. Reduce to a gentle, bubbling simmer and cook for 15–20 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until the dates have dissolved completely into the liquid and the chutney has reduced and thickened. The volume should reduce by roughly a third. As it reduces, taste constantly — the balance should shift from bracingly sour toward sweet-sour-spicy equilibrium.

For a smooth, glossy chutney (the style most commonly served with chaat), pass the hot reduced mixture through a medium sieve, pressing firmly to extract every bit of glossy sauce and leaving any date skins or fibrous bits behind. For a more rustic texture, skip the straining step. Either version is authentic. Taste the strained chutney: at this point it should taste intensely flavored — sweet, sour, spiced, and slightly sulfurous from the kala namak — knowing it will be used as a condiment by the spoonful, not eaten in large quantities.

Transfer the chutney to a clean glass jar and allow to cool to room temperature uncovered. As it cools it will thicken further — a consistency that seems slightly loose when hot is correct; it will reach the drizzling consistency you want once cold. Refrigerate for up to 3 weeks. The flavors deepen and mellow significantly after 24 hours in the refrigerator. Serve drizzled over samosas, pakoras, papdi chaat, or dahi puri — or use it as a meat glaze by warming it briefly and thinning with a little water.

recipes.title: Tarator
recipes.summary: A pale, creamy cold sauce of ground walnuts and tahini emulsified with vinegar and garlic — dense as mayonnaise, nutty and earthy, with a sharp vinegar brightness that cuts through rich fried fish or roasted vegetables.
recipes.description: A pale, creamy cold sauce of ground walnuts and tahini emulsified with vinegar and garlic — dense as mayonnaise, nutty and earthy, with a sharp vinegar brightness that cuts through rich fried fish or roasted vegetables.

ingredients.name: Day-old white bread, crusts removed, torn into pieces

steps.instruction: Spread the walnut halves on a dry baking tray and toast at 175C (350F) for 6-8 minutes, or in a dry skillet over medium heat for 4-5 minutes, stirring occasionally. The walnuts are done when they smell deeply nutty and toasty and have darkened slightly. Cool completely before grinding — warm walnuts will turn oily and paste-like too quickly in the processor.

Place the torn bread pieces in a small bowl and pour the white wine vinegar over them. Turn to coat and let sit for 3-5 minutes until the bread is fully saturated and falling apart. The vinegar-soaked bread acts both as an emulsifier and as a way to introduce the acid smoothly throughout the sauce rather than in harsh pockets.

Combine the cooled toasted walnuts, vinegar-soaked bread, tahini, garlic cloves, and salt in a food processor. Process for 30 seconds until the walnuts are finely ground. With the machine running, add the ice-cold water in a slow stream, then the olive oil. Process until the sauce is smooth, creamy, and homogenous — about 90 seconds total. The cold water is essential: it keeps the walnut oils from separating and produces a stable, mayonnaise-like emulsion. Taste and adjust with more vinegar for sharpness, more water for a looser sauce.

recipes.title: Tempeh Rendang
recipes.summary: Indonesian vegan rendang where slabs of fermented soybean tempeh are slowly simmered in an aromatic coconut milk paste with galangal, lemongrass, and kaffir lime until the coconut cooks dry and the tempeh is encrusted in a dark, burnished spice coating.
recipes.description: Indonesian vegan rendang where slabs of fermented soybean tempeh are slowly simmered in an aromatic coconut milk paste with galangal, lemongrass, and kaffir lime until the coconut cooks dry and the tempeh is encrusted in a dark, burnished spice coating.

ingredients.name: Dried red chilies, soaked and drained

steps.instruction: Blend the soaked dried chilies, shallots, garlic, ginger, coriander, and cumin into a smooth paste in a food processor or blender. Add a tablespoon of water if needed to get it moving. The paste should be fine-textured, deep brick-red, and smell intensely of raw shallot and warm spice.

Heat coconut oil in a large wok or heavy pot over medium heat. Add the paste and fry, stirring constantly, for 8–12 minutes. The paste will first thin out as moisture evaporates, then darken and deepen in color, and finally begin to separate from the oil — a thin ring of clear oil appears around the paste. This is keluarkan minyak — the oil breaking out. This step develops the foundational flavor.

Add tempeh to the fried paste and stir to coat. Pour in coconut milk, add the lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves, turmeric leaf if using, salt, and palm sugar. Stir to combine. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a medium simmer. Cook uncovered, stirring every 10 minutes to prevent sticking.

Continue simmering uncovered for 1–1.5 hours, stirring every 10 minutes with increasing frequency as the liquid reduces. The coconut milk will pass through several stages: creamy white, then pale yellow, then the coconut fat will separate and the paste will begin to fry in its own oil. This final stage — when the rendang is almost dry and the tempeh is frying in coconut oil — develops the characteristic dark, burnished crust. Keep stirring to prevent scorching. The rendang is done when the tempeh is dark and encrusted and the 'sauce' is more of a thick, dark coating.

Transfer to a serving plate or shallow bowl. Scatter fried shallots over the top. Serve with steamed rice, sambal, and pickled cucumber. Rendang improves overnight — the flavors deepen and the spice coating firms.

recipes.title: Tempeh Sambal (Tempe Kering)
recipes.summary: Tempeh sliced thin and fried until golden and nutty, then tossed in a sambal of red chiles, shallots, lemongrass, and kecap manis that caramelizes to a lacquer in the pan — each piece of tempeh absorbing the sweet-spicy glaze while maintaining its characteristic firm, meaty bite. It is one of the great vegan preparations: deeply satisfying in a way that has nothing to do with mimicking meat.
recipes.description: Tempeh sliced thin and fried until golden and nutty, then tossed in a sambal of red chiles, shallots, lemongrass, and kecap manis that caramelizes to a lacquer in the pan — each piece of tempeh absorbing the sweet-spicy glaze while maintaining its characteristic firm, meaty bite. It is one of the great vegan preparations: deeply satisfying in a way that has nothing to do with mimicking meat.

ingredients.name: Coconut or neutral oil for frying
Fresh bay leaves (salam leaves if available)

steps.instruction: Heat 1 cm of oil in a wide skillet over medium-high heat. When the oil shimmers and a small piece of tempeh sizzles immediately on contact, begin frying the tempeh slices in a single layer, without crowding. Fry for 3–4 minutes per side until deep golden-brown and crisp on the outside. The tempeh should not be pale — it needs color for the later glazing step to work properly. Drain on a rack, not paper towels.

In the same pan with the remaining tablespoon of oil, add the shallots and cook over medium heat until golden and beginning to caramelize — about 5 minutes. Add the sliced chiles, garlic, lemongrass, and bay leaves. Stir-fry for 3 minutes until the chiles are softened and fragrant. The shallots should be well beyond translucent — approaching crisp and golden — before the kecap manis is added.

Add the fried tempeh to the sambal base. Pour the kecap manis over everything. Toss vigorously over high heat for 2–3 minutes until the kecap manis caramelizes and coats every piece of tempeh in a dark, glossy glaze. The liquid should reduce completely — the pan should be nearly dry. Season with salt if needed (kecap manis is quite salty already). Remove the lemongrass and bay leaves before serving.

recipes.title: Toasted Farro Salad with Roasted Vegetables
recipes.summary: Whole farro toasted in a dry pan until nutty and golden, then simmered until pleasantly chewy — tossed warm with caramelized roasted vegetables, fresh herbs, lemon, and good olive oil in the manner of Tuscan cucina povera: simply excellent ingredients treated with respect.
recipes.description: Whole farro toasted in a dry pan until nutty and golden, then simmered until pleasantly chewy — tossed warm with caramelized roasted vegetables, fresh herbs, lemon, and good olive oil in the manner of Tuscan cucina povera: simply excellent ingredients treated with respect.

steps.instruction: Place the farro in a large dry skillet over medium heat. Toast, stirring constantly, for 4–6 minutes until the grains smell nutty and are golden — some grains may lightly pop. This step is optional but transforms the flavor dramatically. The toasted grains will have a nuttier, more complex flavor after cooking.

Transfer toasted farro to a pot. Cover with generously salted water or stock (3 parts liquid to 1 part farro by volume). Bring to a boil, reduce to a steady simmer, and cook uncovered for 30–40 minutes for whole farro (20–25 for semi-pearled) until the grains are tender but still have a distinct chew — al dente, like a well-cooked barley. Drain any excess liquid.

Toss all the vegetables with a generous amount of olive oil, salt, and chili flakes on a large sheet pan. Spread in a single layer — do not crowd or they will steam. Roast at 220 C (425 F) for 25–30 minutes, turning once halfway, until caramelized and charred at the edges — particularly the cherry tomatoes, which should burst and concentrate.

While both the farro and vegetables are still warm, combine them in a large bowl. Drizzle with remaining olive oil and lemon juice. Add lemon zest, chili flakes, parsley, mint, and toasted nuts. Toss together gently — you want the warm farro to absorb the lemon and oil. Taste and adjust salt, acid, and oil. The salad is excellent warm, but also very good at room temperature.

recipes.title: Toum
recipes.summary: An entire head of garlic emulsified with oil, lemon, and ice water drop by drop into a billowing, bright-white garlic mousse — intensely pungent yet creamy and light, slathered on grilled meats and wraps.
recipes.description: An entire head of garlic emulsified with oil, lemon, and ice water drop by drop into a billowing, bright-white garlic mousse — intensely pungent yet creamy and light, slathered on grilled meats and wraps.

ingredients.name: Neutral oil (sunflower or light vegetable oil)
Ice water (very cold, with ice cubes nearby)

steps.instruction: Peel all the garlic cloves. Halve each clove lengthwise and use the tip of a paring knife to remove the green germ running through the centre — this is the most important step in making toum that doesn't taste bitter or leave a harsh aftertaste. The germ contains sulfurous compounds that intensify acridly when processed at high speed. Some cooks skip this step; your toum will still emulsify but will taste sharper and more aggressive. Spread the halved cloves on a clean, dry surface.

Place the garlic halves and salt in a food processor. Process for 30 seconds, scraping down the sides every 10 seconds, until the garlic is very finely minced and beginning to form a coarse paste. The salt acts as an abrasive and helps break down the cellular structure before the oil is added. The garlic should look like a fine, wet, slightly sticky mince — not a smooth paste yet, but uniformly broken down. Ensure the bowl and blade are completely dry before this step.

With the food processor running, begin adding the oil in an absolutely tiny stream — a thin trickle, not a pour. Alternate between oil and lemon juice every 30 to 45 seconds, adding ice water when the emulsion looks tight or is struggling to absorb more oil. The total process takes 8 to 12 minutes of continuous processing. The garlic's natural alliinase and stabilising compounds form the emulsifying matrix — there is no egg, no mustard. The emulsion is fragile and temperature-sensitive: keep it cold by working quickly and using ice water. If the mixture looks greasy or separated at any point, stop adding oil and process on while adding a tablespoon of ice water.

Taste the toum and adjust with more lemon juice or salt. The garlic bite should be fierce but not acrid — the emulsification process changes the character of the garlic, making it simultaneously more intense in flavour and somehow less sharp on the palate than raw garlic eaten directly. The lemon should be present as a brightness, not a sourness. Transfer to a clean glass jar. The toum keeps in the refrigerator for up to 4 weeks and remains stable — the cold causes it to firm slightly further, to the consistency of soft lard.

recipes.title: Vegan Green Curry Paste
recipes.summary: A plant-based adaptation that replaces shrimp paste with white miso for umami depth. Same mortar-and-pestle technique, same aromatic intensity, no compromise on funk.
recipes.description: A plant-based adaptation that replaces shrimp paste with white miso for umami depth. Same mortar-and-pestle technique, same aromatic intensity, no compromise on funk.

steps.instruction: Dry-toast coriander seeds in a pan over medium heat, swirling constantly.
In a granite mortar, pound chilies, lemongrass, and galangal hardest first — fibers down to threads.
Add shallot, garlic, and cilantro root. Continue pounding until alliums dissolve into the paste.
Add lime zest, miso, and ground toasted spices. Fold the miso in gently — pounding too hard makes it gummy. Work until the paste is uniform.

recipes.title: Zhug
recipes.summary: Yemen's incendiary green herb sauce — fresh coriander and parsley pounded ferociously with jalapeños, cardamom, and cumin into a thick, emerald-green paste that burns clean and bright. The most beloved condiment across the Yemeni diaspora and every Israeli market stall.
recipes.description: Yemen's incendiary green herb sauce — fresh coriander and parsley pounded ferociously with jalapeños, cardamom, and cumin into a thick, emerald-green paste that burns clean and bright. The most beloved condiment across the Yemeni diaspora and every Israeli market stall.

steps.instruction: In a mortar, pound the cardamom seeds, cumin seeds, and black peppercorns to a fine, even powder. The cardamom seeds are the most important: they must be fully crushed to release the eucalyptus-floral oils that are zhug's signature. If using a spice grinder, run it for 30 seconds and check for any whole seeds remaining. The spice powder should be fine enough to not feel gritty on the tongue.

Add the garlic and salt to the mortar with the ground spices and pound to a smooth paste. Add the jalapeño pieces in two batches, pounding each batch into the garlic base before adding more. Finally, add the coriander and parsley stems first (they are tougher), pound to a rough paste, then add the leaves. Work with a circular grinding motion against the mortar wall between pounding strokes. The paste will be wet and emerald green.

If you haven't yet, add the remaining herb leaves to the paste and work in. Pour the olive oil over the paste and fold it in with a spoon or a few more turns of the pestle. The oil should integrate but not fully emulsify — zhug is not a smooth sauce. Taste and adjust salt and heat. Pack into a clean jar, smoothing the surface, and press a thin layer of olive oil over the top to seal. Refrigerate. Zhug keeps for 1 to 2 weeks and the flavor deepens after 24 hours.
